mcqs.question: What should drive the choice of partition count for a new topic?
options: Target throughput divided by per-partition capacity, plus headroom for growth
The default partition count suggested by the broker's setup wizard
The number of microservices currently deployed in the organization
Whatever count makes the topic name easiest to remember
mcqs.explanation: Sizing from projected throughput against a known per-partition ceiling, with headroom, is the only approach grounded in the actual constraint — since partitions can't shrink and growing them later is disruptive. Defaults, service counts, and naming convenience have no bearing on the real throughput math.

mcqs.question: A consumer group has 30 pods reading from a 10-partition Kafka topic. How many pods are actively processing messages?
options: All 30, since Kafka splits each partition's messages across all available pods
10 — one partition can only be assigned to one consumer within a group at a time, so the other 20 sit idle
0 — a mismatch between pod count and partition count causes the consumer group to fail entirely
20, with 10 pods held in reserve as automatic failover
mcqs.explanation: Kafka's consumer-group protocol assigns each partition to exactly one consumer at a time within a group, so partition count is a hard ceiling on active parallelism — the extra 20 pods here have nothing to do. The group doesn't fail from this mismatch, and there's no partition-splitting or automatic reserve behavior involved.

mcqs.question: A topic is at its partition ceiling and still needs more throughput. What are the real options?
options: Repartition (a planned migration with a consumer-side cutover), or reduce per-message processing cost so each partition does more effective work
Add more consumer pods beyond the partition count, since Kafka will eventually assign them work
Increase the replication factor, which raises the effective partition ceiling
There are no further options once partition count is maxed out for a given broker cluster
mcqs.explanation: Once at the ceiling, the two real levers are a deliberate repartition or cutting the cost of processing each message so existing capacity goes further. Adding pods beyond partition count doesn't help, since idle pods have no partition to read from, and replication factor governs durability, not partition-count-driven parallelism.

mcqs.question: A team provisions exactly the partition count needed for today's load on a topic they already know needs to scale 10x within the year. What does this guarantee?
options: Nothing bad — partition count can always be adjusted later with no operational cost
A disruptive repartition later — exactly the migration that upfront sizing with headroom was meant to avoid
Automatic partition growth once the broker detects sustained high throughput
A compile-time warning from the producer client library
mcqs.explanation: Sizing only for current load on a topic with known future growth locks in a repartition down the line, which is a real, disruptive migration — not a free adjustment. Brokers don't auto-grow partition count based on load, and there's no such compile-time check; this is a capacity-planning decision, not a tooling safeguard.
